title: Getting Started
text:
4.1 Introducing Anaconda

Distribution

A pre-packaged bundle of software that includes the Python interpreter, the standard library, and a variety of additional tools, packages, or utilities
Designed to make installing and using Python easier

Anaconda

A popular open-source Python distribution
Includes conda (package and environment manager), a vast collection of pre-installed scientific computing packages and the Anaconda Navigator
Can download the full distribution or “miniconda”





Anaconda vs. Miniconda

title: Getting Started
text:
4.2 Instructions

Download Anaconda/Miniconda here: Getting Started with Anaconda


4.2.1 Our Recommendation (need at least 10GB of Space)

Our strong recommendation is to install the full Anaconda Distribution, if you have the space.

It will be the easiest to manage, because there is an interface you can use with the “Anaconda Navigator”
Choose the following settings, and follow these instructions: Instruction: Install Python and Related Software





Installing Full Distribution of Anaconda




4.2.2 If you don’t have 10GB of free space…

We need to install miniconda, which is a lightweight version of Anaconda

Unlike the full distribution, miniconda does not come with Jupyter Notebook, an IDE, or most extra packages pre-installed. We have to install those ourselves.



4.2.2.1 Step 1: Install Miniconda

macOSWindows



Go to Miniconda Installer and download the installer for macOS

If you’re not sure whether your Mac has an Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) or Intel chip, check the Apple menu > About This Mac

Open the downloaded .pkg file and follow the installer prompts (defaults are fine)
Open Terminal (search for it with Spotlight, Cmd + Space) and type:
conda --version

If you see a version number printed, the install worked!





Go to Miniconda Installer and download the 64-bit installer for Windows
Run the downloaded .exe file

When prompted, we recommend selecting “Just Me” (not “All Users”)
On the Advanced Options screen, it’s okay to leave “Add Miniconda3 to my PATH environment variable” unchecked. Instead, we’ll use the Anaconda Prompt (installed automatically) to run conda commands

Open the Anaconda Prompt from the Start Menu (search “Anaconda Prompt”) — this is the command line you’ll use for the rest of these steps, instead of the regular Command Prompt or PowerShell
In the Anaconda Prompt, type:
conda --version

If you see a version number printed, the install worked!







4.2.2.2 Step 2: Install Jupyter

In your Terminal (macOS) or Anaconda Prompt (Windows), type:
conda install jupyter

Type y and press Enter when prompted to proceed

Test that it installed correctly:
jupyter notebook --version



4.2.2.3 Step 3: Install VS Code

macOSWindows



Download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com
Open the downloaded .zip file, then drag Visual Studio Code.app into your Applications folder
Open VS Code from Applications or Spotlight




Download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com
Run the downloaded installer

On the “Select Additional Tasks” screen, we recommend checking “Add to PATH” — this lets you open VS Code from the Anaconda Prompt by typing code

Open VS Code once installation finishes






4.2.2.4 Step 4: Set Up VS Code for Python

Open VS Code, and click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (it looks like four squares)
Search for and install:

Python (published by Microsoft)
Jupyter (published by Microsoft)

Open or create a .ipynb (Jupyter Notebook) in VS Code
In the top-right corner, click “Select Kernel” (for a notebook) or check the bottom-right corner for the Python interpreter (for a script)

Choose your base conda environment — it should appear in the list as a conda environment
If you don’t see it, click “Select Another Kernel” > “Python Environments” and look for base

You’re ready to go! Try running a simple cell, e.g. print("hello world"), to confirm everything works

title: Data Types

4.1 Variables and Datatypes

Provide Python code that saves a variable of the following the data types. Then, print the variable. Give a different name to each variable.


int
float
str
list
set
bool
None

For example:

my_int = 5
print(my_int)

my_float = 0.3
print(my_float)

5
0.3

title: Data Types
text:
4.2 Types

Before you run the code in Python, think about what the expected output of these commands is. Once you’ve thought about it, run the code.


type(10.5)

float



type(10)

int



type("7.3")

str



type(8 + 38.1)


type([10, 5])


type("hello")


type(print("hello"))


What happens when you try to apply arithmetic operator to different data types? You can use your previously defined variables to answer this question!

What happens when you multiply a list with an int?
What happens when you add a list with an int?
What happens when you multiply a str with an int?
What happens when you add a str with an int?
What happens when you add a str with an list?


For example, what happens when you run the following code?

my_lst * my_int

The take away message here: When you apply an operator to two different data types, the output might not be obvious! This is called implicit type casting. You can read more about this here.
But if you cannot be bothered/not interested, you should still always check what happens when you combine two data types. Or better yet, you can type cast to make explicit what you’re trying to do!

However, this is not necessary. In fact, Python will still run if the output is not a bool, for example.

def is_anagram(first_word: str, second_word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether two strings are palidrones of each other. 
    An anagram is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to produce another.
    """
    pass


is_anagram('listen', 'silent')

True



is_anagram('listen', 'listened')

False


Challenge question:
Modify your code so that it also ignores spaces and capitalization. For example:

is_anagram('Listen', 'siLeNt')

True



is_anagram('Tom Marvolo Riddle', 'I am Lord Voldemort')

True



Based on the code provided below, write a function that returns True when x is a palindrone. Example input and expected output is provided below.


def is_palindrone(word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether a word is a palindrone
    A palindrone is a word that is spelt the same backwards and forward 
    """
    pass


def is_palindrone(word: str) -> bool:
    return word == word[::-1]


is_palindrone('racecar')


is_palindrone('hello')

title: Lab 04
text:
What are some important components to make a for loop?
Say I have a list sentence = ['Call', 'me', 'Ishmael', '.']. How do I print each word in the list using a for loop?


What does the following code do? What is the expected output?
Discussion Code Block 1:

sentence = ['Call', 'me', 'Ishmael', '.']
for word in sentence:
    if 'l' in word:
        print(word.upper())
    else:
        print(word)

Discussion Code Block 2:

sentence = ['Call', 'me', 'Ishmael', '.']
for i in range(len(sentence)):
    if 'l' in sentence[i]:
        print(sentence[i].upper())
    else:
        print(sentence[i])

Discussion Code Block 3:
What is the difference between the previous code, and the following code? Is there a difference?

sentence = ['Call', 'me', 'Ishmael', '.']
for i in range(len(sentence)):
    if 'l' in sentence[i]:
        sentence[i] = sentence[i].upper()
        print(sentence[i])
    else:
        print(sentence[i])

Discussion Code Block 4:
What about this code block? How is it different to code block 3, and what is the expected output?

sentence = ('Call', 'me', 'Ishmael', '.')
for i in range(len(sentence)):
    if 'l' in sentence[i]:
        sentence[i] = sentence[i].upper()
        print(sentence[i])
    else:
        print(sentence[i])

Discussion Code Block 5 (Challenge!):
What is the expected value of y after running this code, at each print() statement?

x = 10
y = [x, x, x]
print(y)

x = [1, 2, 3]
y = [x, x, x]
print(y)


x[1] = 5
print(y)

The take away message here: When you apply an operator to two different data types, the output might not be obvious! Some operations will work (though it’s not always clear what the final data type will be), while others will raise an error. If it is successful, then the one of the types will be converted to the other. This is called implicit type casting. You can read more about this here.
But if you cannot be bothered/not interested, you should still always check what happens when you combine two data types. Or better yet, you can type cast to make explicit what you’re trying to do!

def frequency(corpus, word):
    """
    Calculates the relative frequency of a word within a corpus. 

    :param corpus: An NLTK Text containing a corpus
    :param word: A word to search for in the corpus

    :return: The proportion of words in corpus that match word
    """
    return corpus.count(word) / len(corpus)

5 Putting it together: Functions, Palindrones, and Anagrams

Based on the code provided below, write a function that returns True when x and y are anagrams of each other, and false otherwise. Example input and expected output is provided below.

Note: You may have noticed : str and -> bool in this sample code. It’s good style to yourself/anyone else using the code that the input parameters should be a str, and the output should be a bool. However, this is not necessary. In fact, Python will still run if the output is not a bool, for example.

def is_anagram(first_word: str, second_word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other. 
    An anagram is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to produce another.
    """
    pass

Possible Solutions:
If there are no duplicates, we can use set() to check if the two words are anagrams of each other.

def is_anagram(first_word: str, second_word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other. 
    An anagram is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to produce another.
    """
    return set(first_word) == set(second_word)

If there are duplicates, we can use sorted() to check if the two words are anagrams of each other.

def is_anagram(first_word: str, second_word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other. 
    An anagram is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to produce another.
    """
    first_word = list(first_word)
    second_word = list(second_word)
    if sorted(first_word) == sorted(second_word):
        return True
    else:
        return False

If you want to be concise, you can also write the above code as:

def is_anagram(first_word: str, second_word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other. 
    An anagram is formed by rearranging the letters of one word to produce another.
    """
    return sorted(list(first_word)) == sorted(list(second_word))


is_anagram('listen', 'silent')

True



is_anagram('listen', 'listened')

False

Based on the code provided below, write a function that returns True when x is a palindrome. Example input and expected output is provided below.

Solution:

def is_palindrone(word: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check whether a word is a palindrone
    A palindrome is a word that is spelt the same backwards and forward 
    """
    return word == word[::-1]


is_palindrone('racecar')

True



is_palindrone('hello')

False
